name: BetaList
tagline: Directory of early-stage startups looking for their first users
startupCost: About $0 (MVP was a customized Tumblr theme)
summary: BetaList features pre-launch and newly launched startups to an audience of early adopters. Marc Köhlbrugge started it in December 2010 on Tumblr. After 10 years it had featured 15,000+ startups, reviewed 70,000+ submissions, and made almost $1M in total revenue. It makes money by charging founders to skip the free review queue and by selling sponsorships.
origin: Köhlbrugge started BetaList in December 2010 to get publicity for an iPad app he and friends were building. The MVP was a Tumblr page with a customized theme. He didn't plan to monetize it until companies started asking how to get featured.
howItMakesMoney: (1) Sponsorship/ad slots: he started at $50/week and doubled the price until buyers said no, ending around $1,500/week. (2) Expedited review: he first did it free as a favor, then charged $15. It later became a paid plan (reported at $99, then $129) to skip the free queue and get featured on a weekday.
growth: A free submission queue with a paid fast lane. The backlog itself creates demand for the paid option.
Early press. Marc wrote 'How I tricked TechCrunch into writing about my startup' about getting coverage early.
Each featured startup shares its listing, which brings in more founders and early-adopter subscribers.
He kept testing prices on ad slots, doubling until demand dropped.
moat: More than a decade of brand recognition in the startup-launch niche, an email and user base of early adopters, and domain authority that makes a listing worth paying for.
risks: Launch directories are easy to start and there are hundreds now. Product Hunt dominates attention, and a directory's value falls if its audience stops engaging.

timeline.event: BetaList launches as a Tumblr site
Marc publishes how he got early TechCrunch coverage
10-year recap: 15,000+ startups featured, 70,000+ submissions reviewed, 100,000+ users, almost $1M total revenue
Paid expedited plan (reported $99, then $129) becomes the main submission product

lessons: A free queue plus a paid skip-the-line option is a simple, scalable way for a directory to make money.
Price ads by doubling until customers say no. His started at $50/week and ended near $1,500/week.
Start with no-code (a Tumblr theme) and rebuild only after demand shows up.
Slow, steady revenue from a directory can fund a solo founder's other projects for a decade.

rebuild.idea: A curated directory of MCP servers and AI-agent tools with verified install and compatibility testing, a free listing queue and a paid expedited review with a badge.
rebuild.why: The number of agent tools and MCP servers is growing fast, and discovery is fragmented across GitHub and X. Builders will pay for fast review and a trustworthy 'tested' badge.
mvp: Scrape GitHub for MCP server repos and seed 300 listings with auto-extracted metadata
Run each through a scripted install test and publish pass/fail
Add a free submit form with a 3-4 week queue and a $49 'review in 48h' option via Stripe
Post the weekly 'new tools' list on X and in AI builder communities to grow the audience
rebuild.fit: An engineer who can automate scraping and testing pipelines and enjoys curation
